pr_comments: I think this is better now. Before I was calling Abort, but that should be called by the server/someone else instead.

issue_context.title: Hub: Closing the browser on a long running task does not trigger OnDisconnectedAsync until after the task has finished
comments:
The fact that `OnDisconnectedAsync` doesn't run until your Hub method returns is by-design. It's all part of the same processing loop.

The ConnectionAborted token should be signalled relatively immediately though. Does it never get signalled or is it taking more time than expected to be signalled? 

> ```cs
> await Task.Delay(1000);
> ```

Does anything change if you pass the `CancellationToken` in here as well? It could be that you're stuck in the delay when the cancellation is triggered.

Thank you for your answer!

> 
> 
> The fact that `OnDisconnectedAsync` doesn't run until your Hub method returns is by-design. It's all part of the same processing loop.
> 
Ah, that's what I suspected.

> The ConnectionAborted token should be signalled relatively immediately though. Does it never get signalled or is it taking more time than expected to be signalled?
> 
It never gets signalled.

> > ```cs
> > await Task.Delay(1000);
> > ```
> 
> Does anything change if you pass the `CancellationToken` in here as well? It could be that you're stuck in the delay when the cancellation is triggered.

No difference, however even without passing the CancellationToken to the Delay function, the delay is only 1 second long, so it should only delay the check by max 1 second.
Thanks for the info! We'll take a look at this. The `ConnectionAborted` token should be something we signal as quickly as possible.

review_comments: Abort should be using HttpContext.Abort (if it's not the fake HttpContext). So even if you keep this, it should result in killing the transport directly.
I'm not sure if calling HttpContesxt.Abort() is the way to do it, but I agree this should also stop the transport if it hasn't stopped already.

> this should also stop the transport if it hasn't stopped already.

That's the part I don't have currently

Is there a race with HttpContext.Abort and Kestrel writing the bytes in the response stream to the network? As soon as I added this it started randomly failing tests that were looking for a close message.

I wouldn't call it a race as much as behaving as intended. Aborting drops any unflushed bytes in Kestrel's internal buffers. If you want to guarantee delivery of the bytes you've written, you cannot abort. This is the same reason why we cannot reliably abort a SignalR connection and send a CloseMessage.

> I'm not sure if calling HttpContesxt.Abort() is the way to do it

Apparently it isn't.
So do we need to abort the HttpContext? Or can we assume the server will clean up correctly when we return from the middleware?

The server should do the right thing to complete the request and/or close the connection when middleware completes. If the client receives data slower the configured rate limit, the server will abort the connection.
